To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
temperature‐related shifts in the phenology of butterflies are affected by habitat type, and that habitat type can affect the phenology of a species, even if the temperature is the same.
temperature‐related shifts in the seasonal appearance of butterflies depend on the habitat type.
the timing of seasonal events in butterfly species is affected by both ambient temperature and habitat.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of climate change on phenology and distribution of butterflies.
the question how climate and land use interact in affecting the phenology of butterflies.
the effects of global climate and habitat changes on phenological shifts and their implications for conservation management.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
temperature‐related shifts in the phenology of butterflies are habitat‐dependent.
climate and land‐cover changes have interacting effects on species phenology.
the phenological advancement of species in response to climate change is not uniform across habitat types, and that phenology studies should be conducted in a habitat‐specific context.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
phenological responses of butterfly species to temperature and habitat type depend on each other.
phenology is affected by climate, but that the response is dependent on habitat type.
the effects of climate warming on the phenology and abundance are habitat‐dependent.
The main takeaway from our work is that
phenology of butterflies can be affected by both climate and habitat type.
phenological studies should consider the habitat type in which the species is found.
phenological responses to temperature are not the same in all habitats and that phenology of species may change differently in different habitat types.
